title: What a wealth tax looks like in the age of AI billionaires | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

Anthropic’s initial public offering has created overnight multi-millionaires (and some billionaires), and the timing is complicated.

They are coming into incredible wealth just as some states are trying different forms of wealth taxes, fueled bya shrinking middle classand growing unease about the concentration of wealth and power.

New York City is about to chargean extra yearly taxon expensive homes that aren’t anyone’s primary residence. Washington, DC is considering a tax on investment income for wealthier households. Washington state will levy its first modern income tax on households making more than $1 million in 2028.

California’s Prop 40 “billionaire tax” failed on Election Day, but Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D- MD) told Politico that the failure of Prop 40 suggestsone state can’t do it alone. A bill introduced in both the House and Senate alreadyproposes a 5% taxon the net worth of America’s billionaires, which could become a flashpoint in the 2028 presidential election.

Prop 40’s defeat — and the sudden emergence of a new class of AI elite — has simply launched a more heated national debate about how exactly the rich should be taxed.

“If someone’s worth $1 billion, that doesn’t mean that they have $50 million of cash around to pay the tax,” said Anderson Lafontant, managing director of Blue Zone Wealth Advisors.

Lafontant, whose clients include employees of AI companies, said a lot ofthis net worth is mostly on paper. Companies in IPO scenarios have restrictions on when shareholders can sell stock after it goes public, so an employee may not hold much liquid cash until their shares are sold. (Lafontant does not currently work with any Anthropic employees or founders.)

Prop 40 would have levied a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires who lived in California on January 1, 2026, not counting real estate or most retirement accounts.

“That’s the point about a wealth tax, is it hits paper wealth,” said Tom Steyer, billionaire climate activist and former California gubernatorial candidate. He argues that a person could borrow against stock to pay taxes. He called Prop 40 “imperfect” but “better than nothing.”

Megan Lisa Jones, a private wealth and tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said some of her clients have left or talked about leaving California to seek better tax rates and avoid a potential Prop 40. Lafontant also said some of her clients have moved for tax reasons, though not necessarily over a wealth tax.

Both said their high-net worth clients did not want to speak with CNN.

“Some of my clients would say, ‘Well, I can’t leave now, but I’ll leave in four years…and I’m not a billionaire yet, so I don’t need to worry about it yet.’ But if they tax the billionaires, it’s just a question of time before it starts trickling down and taxes everyone,” Jones said.

Steyer has said a national wealth tax would be better, so the wealthy don’t keep moving to find tax havens.

“I’m not mad at people for being rich. It’s just that people are really suffering on the other end,” he said.

California Governor-elect Xavier Becerra has called Prop 40 “sketchy policy”and said the state needs a long-term solution instead of a one-time affair.

His spokesperson told CNN in a statement that the success of Prop 3, a state measure that made extra taxes on high-income earners permanent, is proof that California voters support taxing the rich.

Washington state voters upheld a so-called “millionaires’ tax” on Election Day, where any income over $1 million will get taxed. This means two spouses each making more than $500,000 would be taxed like millionaires.

There is currently no income tax in Washington state. Pending a constitutional challenge, this tax of 9.9% goes into effect in 2028.

That has prompted Michelle Dellino, a family law attorney in Seattle, to advise her clients to think through big life decisions.

“Some of those choices — like marrying, signing a prenup or moving —can’t really easily be undone,” she said.

Some of her clients might also be subject to a “scary” tax bill when company stock vests and is taxed like salary, even if the employee doesn’t have cash from selling those shares.

The soaring cost of living nationwide raises questions about whether being a millionaire still holds the financial significance it once did. For example, the median single-family home in Seattle sold for about $1.1 million in October, according toan analysisby JanusGroup Real Estate.

Lafontant said those who own assets in America are winners, “and if you’re not an asset owner, you are just getting gobbled up by inflation.”

If a “wealth tax” is implemented she said she’d prefer to see taxes levied when people sell assets, not when they’re holding them.

As AI changes society, Jones poses a broader question about the American tax policy relying heavily on ordinary income.

“If we don’t have people working the same way, if AI really does replace jobs, then we’re going to have another big challenge with our tax system and how we’re going to fund things,” she said.
